topic: Constexpr Functions in C++11 versus C++14
explanation:
A key aspect of constexpr functions is that their implementation restrictions were significantly relaxed in C++14 compared to C++11, dramatically improving their usability. In both versions, a constexpr function can produce compile-time results when given compile-time arguments, but can also operate at runtime like a normal function when given runtime arguments.

Scott Meyers emphasizes this evolution as a critical step in making compile-time programming more accessible and practical. The C++11 restrictions forced a functional programming style that was often unnatural for C++ developers, whereas the C++14 changes allow for conventional, imperative-style code, lowering the barrier to adoption.

The mechanics in C++11 were highly constrained: a constexpr function could contain only a single executable statement, which had to be a return statement. To implement any meaningful logic, developers had to rely on workarounds like the ternary conditional operator for if-else logic and recursion for loops. In C++14, these limitations were mostly removed. A C++14 constexpr function can contain local variables, if statements, switch statements, and loops like for and while, making the code vastly more readable and easier to write and maintain.

This evolution has profound practical implications. Algorithms that were cumbersome or convoluted to implement in C++11's restrictive style became straightforward in C++14. This encourages developers to move more logic from runtime to compile time, resulting in faster programs and the ability to catch certain errors during compilation. For example, parsing a simple configuration string or calculating lookup tables at compile time becomes a much more tenable task.

The most common pitfall is being unaware of these differences. A developer familiar only with C++11 might avoid constexpr for moderately complex logic, believing it's impossible. Conversely, writing C++14-style constexpr functions will cause compilation failures if the project must be compatible with an older, C++11-only compiler, making knowledge of the standard's version essential.
practical_example: When creating a compile-time lookup table, such as for a sine function, the C++14 standard allows you to write a clear, iterative loop to populate the table within a constexpr function, whereas in C++11 you would have been forced to write a more complex recursive template meta-program or recursive function.
keywords: constexpr C++11 C++14, C++14 constexpr relaxation, C++14 multi-statement constexpr, compile-time execution
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
